passage:
Tuesday, 11 pm
Shankar did it again at dinner. Someone mentioned a new restaurant and he said, "Madhav wouldn't know, he's never eaten with a fork," and the table laughed. I laughed too. I always laugh.
Now I'm lying here doing the maths. If I say something tomorrow, will it become a big scene? Will they say I can't take a joke? Maybe I am oversensitive. It was one line. But it's also the fourth line this month, and I've noticed I've stopped ordering anything unfamiliar when we go out, just in case.
Option 1: say it privately to Shankar. Option 2: let it go and save my energy for exams.
Both seem fine. Neither feels light. What's tiring is carrying it around all night like this, deciding.
Maybe I'll talk to Shankar after the morning lab.

qa.q: What did Shankar say about Madhav at dinner?
qa.a: He said Madhav wouldn't know, he's never eaten with a fork.

qa.q: What worries Madhav about speaking up tomorrow?
qa.a: He worries it will become a big scene, that they'll say he can't take a joke, and that maybe he is oversensitive.

qa.q: Madhav is leaning towards talking to Shankar after the morning lab. Why is that a reasonable choice, alongside letting it go?
qa.a: A private word could stop the pattern without a scene; letting it go is also valid, but a sleepless night shows that silence has a cost too.

qa.q: How might Shankar react if Madhav raises it privately?
qa.a: Shankar might be defensive at first, but he may not realise his jokes have piled up, and hearing about the fourth line might surprise him.

grounding: A young adult hears a demeaning joke about his background and weighs whether speaking up is worth the friction, tired from carrying it.

passage: The bus to the district college was late again, and the tea-stall owner at the kasba stand had an opinion, as always. "Two years of college, and then? Rotis are rotis, beti, degree or no degree." The men on the bench chuckled. Zeenat's hand tightened on her file. Dilnaz glanced at her, waiting. Zeenat could say it: that she had topped the first-year accounts exam, that her rotis were none of his business. But the bus was coming, he gave her father credit in bad months, and she'd have to stand here every morning. Was it even worth it? Maybe she was being too touchy. She said nothing and climbed on. At the window, Dilnaz squeezed her hand. "You can say it tomorrow. Or never. Both are fine." Zeenat nodded, but the sentence sat in her chest all the way to college.

qa.a: She had topped the first-year accounts exam.

qa.a: It leaves the decision with Zeenat and treats both speaking and staying quiet as legitimate, instead of adding pressure.

qa.q: How might the tea-stall owner see his own remark?
qa.a: He probably thinks it was harmless teasing, not realising how it sits with Zeenat all the way to college.

passage: On the third day of his placement on a hospital ward in Leeds, Gabriel was changing a dressing when Nadia, his mentor, breezed past and told the patient, "Don't mind him, he's our male nurse. Couldn't get into medicine, bless him." The patient chuckled. Gabriel kept his hands steady. It wasn't true; nursing had been his first choice since he'd sat by his grandfather's bed at fourteen. On the bus home he turned it over and over. Was he being touchy? She'd said it with a smile. If he raised it, she'd be signing off his competencies next week. If he didn't, he'd hear it again, and again he'd smile. He typed her a message, deleted it, typed a shorter one. His thumb hovered. Then he slid the phone into his pocket, too tired to decide tonight, and rested his forehead against the cold window.

qa.q: What did Nadia tell the patient about Gabriel?
qa.a: "Don't mind him, he's our male nurse. Couldn't get into medicine, bless him."

qa.q: What was Gabriel worried about as he weighed whether to speak up?
qa.a: He wondered if he was being touchy, and he worried that raising it with his mentor could cost him, since she would be signing off his competencies next week.

qa.q: With his thumb over the message, what choices did Gabriel have, and what would each cost?
qa.a: He could send a short, calm message or ask for a quiet word, risking friction; or let it go for now, which avoids conflict but may mean carrying the same remark again. Either is a fair choice.

qa.q: How might Nadia see things if Gabriel never mentions it?
qa.a: Nadia would likely think it was harmless teasing and keep repeating it, never knowing it followed Gabriel all the way home on the bus.

grounding: A nursing student hears a demeaning remark from his mentor and weighs whether speaking up is worth the friction, while silence is already wearing on him.

passage: The placement cell smelt of toner and old files. Hansa handed over her form for the core mechanical drive, and the officer, not unkindly, slid a second sheet across. "Take the HR one also, beta. Girls finally settle there, no? Less pressure." Behind her, Lalremsiami stopped scrolling. Hansa felt heat climb her neck. Four years of lathe work, a gold in the design project. Was she overreacting to one tired man's habit? He signed the shortlists, and twenty people were in the queue. Staying quiet would be easy; she'd been doing it since first year, and it was getting heavy. She pushed the HR sheet back, gently. "Only mechanical, sir. That's the job I want." He shrugged and stamped her form. Outside, her hands were shaking. Lalremsiami bumped her shoulder. "Okay?" "Ask me tomorrow," Hansa said, and laughed, a little.

qa.q: What did the officer slide across to Hansa?
qa.a: A second sheet, the HR form.

qa.q: Why did Hansa hesitate before answering the officer?
qa.a: She wondered whether she was overreacting to one tired man's habit, and she knew he signed the shortlists, so speaking up might cost her.

qa.q: What choice did Hansa make at the turning point, and why did it suit the moment?
qa.a: She pushed the HR sheet back and calmly said she only wanted mechanical, a short, clear reply that stated what she wanted without starting a fight in front of the queue.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have experienced watching the exchange?
qa.a: Lalremsiami noticed at once and stopped scrolling; the shoulder bump afterwards shows they understood the small reply had cost Hansa something.

passage: I remember the moment clearly, even two years later. It was my first term at the Delhi college. In the corridor, a senior said loudly, "Madrasi girl, bring us some idli tomorrow," and his friends laughed. I'm from Coimbatore, and I'm not a "Madrasi," and nobody there calls us that. I froze. Part of me wanted to say, "Please don't call me that." Part of me thought, am I overreacting? It's just a joke. Will they make my life hard if I speak? I said nothing and walked on. That night I told Imran, my classmate, and he said, "You don't have to fight every battle. But you don't have to swallow it either." I didn't sleep much. A week later, when it happened again, I said calmly, "My name's Kavitha." They stopped. Both choices were mine. Carrying the silence had been heavier.

qa.q: What did the senior call Kavitha?
qa.a: He called her "Madrasi girl."

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when she froze?
qa.a: Kavitha felt hurt and unsure, torn between speaking up and worrying about overreacting or causing trouble.

qa.q: What did Imran's advice help Kavitha see?
qa.a: That staying silent or speaking up are both valid choices, and that she didn't have to swallow the hurt every time.

qa.q: How might the seniors have felt when Kavitha said her name?
qa.a: They may have felt caught off guard, realising their joke wasn't welcome, and so they stopped.

grounding: A young adult hears a demeaning nickname, weighs whether to speak and whether she is overreacting, and finds that carrying silence is tiring.

passage:
Internship mentor's note, Thursday.
Mridul (third-year, marketing intern) came to see me after the team lunch. A senior manager had said to him, "You people from small towns are very hardworking, not like the city kids." Mridul told me he wasn't sure whether to say anything. "Maybe it was a compliment? Maybe I'm being too sensitive?" He also worried about his placement if he complained. He said he'd felt oddly small all afternoon. I told him either choice was legitimate: he could raise it calmly, or let it go, and I'd support him either way. I also said that if he stays silent, he doesn't have to pretend it didn't sting. He decided to let it pass for now but asked if we could meet weekly. I've agreed and noted the comment in case of a pattern.
- Nandini

qa.a: He said, "You people from small towns are very hardworking, not like the city kids."

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling after the lunch?
qa.a: Mridul felt oddly small and unsure, wondering if he was being too sensitive and worried about his placement.

qa.q: What did Nandini do that supported Mridul?

qa.q: How might the senior manager have seen the comment?

passage:
Tuesday night
In tutorial today Naveen said, "For a girl from a small town, you're really confident." Everyone smiled like it was a nice thing. I smiled too. Now I'm lying here thinking about it.
Was it nice? Or did he mean small-town girls are usually scared? Am I making it bigger than it is?
If I say something tomorrow, he'll say "I was praising you," and I'll look touchy. If I don't, it just sits in my stomach with all the other little ones.
I think I'll ask him, lightly, "What did you mean about small-town girls?" If he meant well, fine. If not, at least he'll think.
Either way, I'm allowed to be tired of it.
- Elizabeth

qa.q: What did Naveen say in the tutorial?
qa.a: Naveen said, "For a girl from a small town, you're really confident."

qa.q: How does Elizabeth feel lying awake?
qa.a: Elizabeth feels unsure and tired, wondering if she is overreacting while the remark sits heavily with other small ones.

qa.q: Why is asking Naveen "What did you mean?" a reasonable approach?
qa.a: It lets Elizabeth raise the issue lightly, gives Naveen a chance to explain, and avoids assuming the worst.

qa.q: How might Naveen react if Elizabeth asks him?
qa.a: Naveen might be surprised, but the question could help him notice how his compliment carried a stereotype.

passage:
In the block office of a small town in Bundelkhand, Kashish had joined as a young development officer. At the Monday meeting, the senior clerk looked at her file and said, "Madam, why so much planning? You'll get married next year and leave anyway." The men around the table chuckled.
Kashish's cheeks burned. Should she say something? The clerk had been there for twenty years. He was the one who'd have to help her with every file.
Later, Sarita, the only other woman on staff, found her on the verandah. "It happens every time. You don't have to answer it today."
"But if I never say anything, I'll carry it every Monday."
Sarita nodded. "Then say it simply. One line. I'll be in the room."

qa.q: How long had the senior clerk been there?
qa.a: He had been there for twenty years.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when her cheeks burned?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt, and unsure whether speaking up was worth the friction with someone she depended on.

qa.q: What makes Sarita's advice helpful?
qa.a: Sarita says it's okay not to answer today, and offers support if Kashish chooses one simple line, leaving the choice to Kashish.

qa.q: How does Sarita seem to see the remark?
qa.a: Sarita sees it as a familiar pattern that happens every time, and she feels ready to stand with Kashish.

passage:
Yuki was born in Manchester and had lived there all her life. At her first office job, a colleague handed back her report and said, cheerfully, "Your English is really good! Where did you learn it?"
"Here," Yuki said. "In Manchester."
The colleague laughed and walked off.
At lunch, Yuki told Lindiwe. "Should I have said more? Or am I making something out of nothing?"
"You're not," Lindiwe said. "I get 'you're so articulate' all the time."
"If I speak up, I'm the difficult new girl. If I don't, I carry it home."
"Both are allowed," Lindiwe said. "You don't owe anyone a lesson today."
Yuki nodded. She still felt tired.

qa.q: Where was Yuki born?
qa.a: She was born in Manchester.

qa.q: What is Yuki feeling as she talks to Lindiwe at lunch?
qa.a: Yuki feels tired and unsure, wondering whether she overreacted and whether speaking up is worth being seen as difficult.

qa.q: What does Lindiwe's advice offer Yuki?
qa.a: It tells Yuki both choices are allowed, so she doesn't have to feel guilty whichever she picks.

qa.q: How might the colleague see the comment about Yuki's English?
qa.a: The colleague probably meant it as a friendly compliment and didn't notice it treated Yuki as a foreigner.

Something's been going round my head all week. In chemistry lab on Monday, Professor Sethi said, when I came in two minutes late, "Your people always run on your own time, no?" A few people laughed. I laughed too, which I hate. I've been deciding since then whether to say something. Part of me thinks I'm making a mountain out of it; it was one line. Part of me knows it wasn't the first. If I speak to him, he might mark me as difficult. If I don't, I carry it. Honestly the carrying is heavy. I might ask to see him after class and just ask what he meant. Or I might not. Imran

Monday, the week before winter exams. In the library queue Kalyani laughs, "Tanuja, say 'hospital' again, it's so cute, so village!" Two others giggle. Tanuja smiles, says nothing, and her cheeks stay hot through the whole chapter she is meant to be reading.
